Filters can pay only at merges where most matched pairs have the wrong split pattern, and do pay where such merges bind; we show both where this holds and where it fails. A survival recursion justifies the accounting, a symmetry lemma shows that the filters cannot bias the planted solution, and simulations support the remaining heuristics.

item.title: Parallelizable modes for duplex-based authenticated encryption
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2801
Authors: Joan Daemen, Silvia Mella, Gilles Van Assche
Summary: This note enriches the SHAKE and TurboSHAKE-based authenticated encryption schemes defined by Daemen et al. at EuroS&P 2025 with parallelizable ones, while keeping their security properties. The main contribution is a new deck cipher mode, called FlightDeck, that has the ability of processing input strings similarly to KangarooTwelve and producing output strings as in counter mode, so both parallelizable. We then instantiate FlightDeck on top of the overwrite duplex (OD) construction, in turn on top of a Keccak-p permutation. Combined with a deck cipher-based mode like Deck-BO, the security of the resulting authenticated encryption schemes reduces to the PRF security of keyed (Turbo)SHAKE and to the collision resistance of (Turbo)SHAKE. Compared to the schemes defined at EuroS&P 2025, replacing UpperDeck with FlightDeck greatly improves their software efficiency as one can implement them with Keccak-p permutations evaluated in parallel.

item.title: Testing CCZ-equivalence to permutations via projections of Walsh zero spaces, with applications to APN functions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2800
Authors: Emanuele Bellini
Summary: Whether almost perfect nonlinear (APN) permutations exist in even dimension $n\ge 8$ is a long-standing open question, the big APN problem. The only example known in even dimension, on six bits, was found from a quadratic APN function that is not itself a permutation, by Carlet--Charpin--Zinoviev (CCZ) equivalence. It is therefore natural to test APN functions for CCZ-equivalence to a permutation. This amounts to finding two complementary $n$-dimensional subspaces among the zeros of the Walsh transform, which lie in $\mathbb{F}_2^{2n}$. A known necessary condition only uses their projections to $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and cannot decide every case. We give an exact test for functions whose Walsh supports are affine, including all quadratic functions. It reconstructs the subspaces from their projections, through searches for subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and for constrained bilinear maps. On the benchmarked functions in dimension twelve, it lists them $39$ to $55$ times faster than the generic search of the commonly used sboxU library. We then study the functions $x^3+a^{-1}\mathrm{Tr}(a^3x^9)$, which Göloğlu and Pavlů proved not to be CCZ-equivalent to permutations when $4$ divides $n$. With their result, our computations show that this holds for every even $n\le 24$. In dimension $18$ the necessary condition is satisfied, and the new test decides the case. We conjecture this for every even dimension. We also compile $25$ classes of quadratic APN functions in dimension ten from published instances, with equivalence certificates. No function in these classes or in their switching closure is CCZ-equivalent to a permutation. All code and data are public.

item.title: Exploring the Set of APN Functions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2799
Authors: Jules Baudrin, Pierre Galissant, Léo Perrin
Summary: An Almost Perfect Nonlinear (APN) function $F : \mathbb{F}_2^n \to \mathbb{F}_2^n$ provides optimal protection against differential attacks, meaning that the equation $F(x+a)=F(x)+b$ has at most 2 solutions~$x$ when $a \neq 0$. Setting aside some sporadic examples, such functions are hard to find in practice, and whether there exists APN bijections of $ \mathbb{F}_2^n$ when $n > 6$ is even (the Big APN Problem) is still unknown.
In this paper, we provide the tools needed to explore the complete set of known APN functions. Indeed, for a given APN function $F$, we in fact know many: all functions CCZ-equivalent to $F$ are also APN, and so are its switching neighbours. These notions have been in the literature for many years, but several unknowns remain that complicate the exploration of the corresponding functions in practice: a given function has too many switching neighbours, and the algorithms that are known to iterate through a CCZ-equivalence class return multiple representatives per extended-affine (EA) equivalence class.
We solve both problems. First, we show how to partition precisely the CCZ-equivalence class of a quadratic APN function in practice, and thus obtain exactly one representative per EA-equivalence class. To achieve this, we carefully investigate the set of the automorphisms of the graph of a quadratic APN function, and show how to generate them very efficiently using the ortho-derivative. Second, we provide the first detailed investigation of the set of the switching neighbours of a function, show in particular how an overwhelming majority of them are trivial, and explain how to get rid of those. Incidentally, we build a new extended-affine equivalence class invariant using the resulting set of non-trivial switching neighbours.
For both theoretical contributions, we pushed highly-efficient and easy to re-use implementations of the corresponding algorithms to the sboxU library. It allowed us to generate databases containing all known APN functions for $n=6$ and $n=7$. For $n=8$, our algorithms are efficient-enough that we can investigate the properties of the millions of quadratic APN function recently exhibited. In the process, we generate a few thousands of new CCZ-equivalence classes.
In the light of our work, the successes of the exploration strategies for $n=6$ (i.e. finding an APN function inequivalent to any monomial and quadratic mapping, and finding an APN bijection in even dimension) seems to be an artifact due to the small dimension that we show not to work for dimension 8 and which we do not expect to work either when the dimension is greater.

item.title: More Salt, Please: A Simple Compiler for Post-Quantum Strong aPAKE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2798
Authors: William Riccardo Duro, Sebastian Faller, Julia Hesse, Máté Horváth
Summary: Resistance to precomputation attacks is a central security goal in password-based cryptography, as it drastically increases the runtime of brute-force attacks on breached password hashes. Strong asymmetric password-authenticated key exchange (saPAKE), which enforces such precomputation resistance, is standardized by the IRTF and deployed today at large scale. Unfortunately, no practical and easy-to-deploy saPAKE exists yet that withstands quantum attackers. Current constructions use rate-limiting tools such as oblivious pseudo-random functions (OPRFs), of which post-quantum versions are significantly more costly and complex than their discrete-log based counterparts.
In this paper, we take a new approach to precomputation resistance. Starting from the compilers from PAKE to aPAKE by Gentry-MacKenzie-Ramzan (Crypto 2006) and Liu-Lyu-Han (Asiacrypt 2024), we propose a password file ratchet that adds precomputation resistance to these compilers through continuously updating the password file. The update is a simple salted hash. With a variety of practical post-quantum PAKEs at hand, this yields a ready-to-deploy post-quantum saPAKE at the trade-off of a changing server state.

item.title: The Maximum Possible Nonlinearity for a Balanced Boolean Function in 10 Variables is 492
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2797
Authors: Youle Xu, Qichun Wang
Summary: Determining the maximum nonlinearity of 10-variable balanced Boolean functions has been a long-standing open problem. In this paper, we resolve it by proving that the maximum nonlinearity is exactly 492, thereby confirming Dobbertin’s conjecture in dimension 10. To exclude nonlinearity 494, we derive a quadratic residue for the Walsh spectrum and refine a local energy table from four-block concatenation by retaining the signs of the Walsh coefficients. The resulting bounds exclude all but the largest polar rank; a product inequality and a parity argument eliminate the remaining case.

item.title: Applying Combinatorial Techniques To Find Minimal Non-Complete Set Coverings
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2796
Authors: Enrico Piccione, Jan Vorloeper
Summary: One of the most prominent hardware countermeasures against side-channel attacks are threshold implementations (TIs). The technique uses masking to split the operations in a cryptographic algorithm into several ones operating on shares. The coverage and non-completeness requirements of TIs are mathematically described by the notion of non-complete set coverings (NCSCs). Importantly, the number of members inside an NCSC determines the number of output shares and therefore directly impacts the complexity of the resulting TI.
In this work, we derive new lower bounds on the minimal number of members of NCSCs and obtain new upper bounds by explicit constructions. We present a group-theoretic construction of balanced NCSCs, in which the numbers of input and output shares coincide, together with a search algorithm based on intersections of group translates. Our methods determine the smallest balanced coverings in two previously unresolved cases and yield exact minima and classifications of optimal coverings for an infinite family of parameters. These results resolve all four explicit open problems posed by Farr\`as, Fidalgo and Lara-Nino.

item.title: Exploiting Matrix-Vector Multiplication in AIMer: Single-Trace Attacks on Key Generation and Signing
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2795
Authors: Süleyman Emir Akın, Abdullah Talayhan, Özcan Öztürk
Summary: This paper presents two side-channel attacks against AIMer v3.0, one of the two signature schemes selected in the Korean Post-Quantum Cryptography (KpqC) competition. Both are single-trace attacks that recover the full secret key without a profiling phase, one against key generation and one against signing. Both target the same routine: the matrix-vector multiplication invoked by either phase expands each bit of its secret operand into an all-zero or an all-one mask, which then gates the accumulation of the corresponding public matrix row. A single execution therefore leaks one distinguishable segment per secret bit. What makes the attacks non-profiled is that each attacked trace carries its own labelled training set. During key generation, creating the dense invertible public matrices invokes the matrix-vector multiplication routine hundreds of times, on operands that are public. In signing the same derivation takes place, and in addition the signature itself opens all but one of the $N$ parties of every repetition, so the bits of nearly every multiplication in the trace are public. In both attacks we use a supervised classifier to recover the unknown value. In key generation that value is the private key itself, whereas in signing there are three distinct routes to it: the key itself, a party's share of the key, and a party's share of an S-box output. Recovering any one of them is enough to recover the private key. We validate both attacks on an ARM Cortex-M4: one trace recovers the exact secret key from every capture we took, $100$ key generations for each of AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256, and $100$ signatures for each of AES-128f, AES-192f and AES-256f. We also discuss possible countermeasures.

item.title: BeaverDam: A Post-Quantum Threshold Key Recovery Protocol from a One-Time Threshold Oblivious Random Function
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2794
Authors: Benedikt Auerbach, Shuichi Katsumata, Kaoru Takemure, Ida Tucker
Summary: Secure backups are a practical necessity of E2EE messaging apps, typically relying on password-protected key-recovery (PPKR) protocols. These allow users to turn a human-memorable password into a cryptographic key with the help of a server. Recently, Signal and Juicebox proposed threshold PPKR (tPPKR) protocols, removing the trust on a centralized server. Unfortunately, known solutions are only classically secure, lagging behind the shift toward post-quantum (PQ), or to be more precise, hybrid secure E2EE.
We present BeaverDam, a novel tPPKR protocol that is PQ secure with efficiency close to existing classical protocols. It also easily extends to hybrid security, standing as the first concretely efficient hybrid-secure tPPKR protocol. BeaverDam relies on a new primitive we introduce --- one-time threshold oblivious random functions (tORF). Unlike full-fledged OPRFs, which are notoriously difficult to construct in a PQ-secure manner, one-time tORF offers weaker but sufficient security guarantees tailored to the tPPKR setting.
We then construct an efficient one-time tORF called Beaver, inspired by multi-party computation (MPC) techniques. Owing to the one-time feature, we only need to securely compute a 2-wise independent hash function, making our protocol very efficient. We conclude by presenting a practical instantiation of BeaverDam and comparing its performance to state-of-the-art classical tPPKR protocols, namely Signal's SVR3 and Juicebox.

item.title: Weights Come Almost for Free in Ramp Threshold Cryptography
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2793
Authors: Aarushi Goel, Mingyuan Wang
Summary: A weighted threshold access structure assigns a weight to each party and authorizes a subset of parties whenever their total weight exceeds a prescribed threshold. Most existing approaches to designing multiparty cryptographic protocols in the weighted threshold setting, however, either incur complexity that grows with the total weight assigned to the parties or remain far from concretely efficient.
Toward \emph{concretely efficient} weighted threshold primitives, we take a different route and relax to the \emph{ramp} setting, in which two thresholds are prescribed: a subset whose total weight falls below an $\alpha$ fraction of the total is unauthorized, while a subset whose total weight exceeds a $\beta$ fraction is authorized. Exploiting the gap between these two thresholds, we obtain the following results.
1. Given any weighted ramp threshold access structure with privacy threshold $\alpha$ and reconstruction threshold $\beta$, where $0\!<\!\alpha\!<\!\beta\!<\!1$, we present a weight compression technique that reduces the total weight to $\approx n/(2(\beta-\alpha))$ while preserving the authorized and unauthorized sets. Combined with the standard player-virtualization paradigm, this yields concretely efficient weighted threshold cryptographic protocols with only a multiplicative overhead of $\approx 1/(2(\beta-\alpha))$ over their unweighted counterparts. Previously, the best known compression technique in this setting, due to Benhamouda et al.~[ITC'23], achieved total weight $\approx 5n/(\beta-\alpha)$.
2. Player virtualization has an inherent drawback: a party's share size and workload grow in proportion to its (compressed) weight, so the parties in which the most trust is placed also bear the largest computational and communication costs. Thus, although the \emph{overall} overhead is $O(1)$, the cost borne by a single party can still be $O(n)$ times that in the unweighted setting. Our second result removes this imbalance. Building on our compression technique, we construct a linear secret-sharing scheme in which every party receives a share of size $\widetilde{O}(1)$, independent of its weight, for a total share size of $\widetilde{O}(n)$, nearly matching the $O(n)$ complexity of standard unweighted threshold secret sharing.

item.title: Independent Leakage Does Not Save Evasive LWE: Refuting Folklore Fixes in the Private-Coin Setting
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2792
Authors: Yao-Ching Hsieh
Summary: The evasive learning with errors (evasive LWE) assumption has enabled a wide range of advanced cryptographic constructions from lattices in the past few years. The simple intuition that LWE remains secure even when additional ``non-zeroizing'' short preimages are given has proved highly versatile in applications. Unfortunately, recent counterexamples have refuted its general private-coin formulations, showing that having the short preimages along with arbitrary auxiliary leakage about the secret and target matrices can invalidate this intuition.
To preserve important applications, particularly witness encryption, the community has sought to repair the assumption by restricting the allowed leakage. One folklore proposal requires the secret and target matrices, together with their respective leakage, to be generated independently. This restriction appears to preserve the application to witness encryption while ruling out all previously known counterexamples.
In this work, we refute this proposal. Assuming LWE and indistinguishability obfuscation, we show that both the binding and hiding variants of private-coin evasive LWE are false even with the independent sampler restriction. Our counterexamples exploit only auxiliary leakage about the target matrix. We sample the secret honestly from a standard uniform or Gaussian distribution, independently of the target and its leakage, and we use no auxiliary information about the secret.

item.title: New Results in Adaptively-Secure Broadcast Encryption and Succinct Computational Secret Sharing from Standard Lattices
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2791
Authors: Rishab Goyal, Saikumar Yadugiri
Summary: Projective pseudorandom generators (PPRGs), introduced by [Applebaum et al.; STOC'23], expand a short seed into a long pseudorandom string, with a special feature that one can generate a short $\textit{projected}$ key, for any set $S$, such that it reveals the output bits in $S$ while preserving pseudorandomness of the remaining bits. They demonstrated that PPRGs can bypass the 'representation size barrier' in computational secret sharing schemes, and designed PPRGs assuming hardness of a variety of standard cryptographic assumptions. Later, [Hsieh, Waters, and Wu; EUROCRYPT'25] showed that PPRGs can also be used to design adaptively-secure broadcast encryption in the standard model, without relying on unprovable heuristics.
In this work, we design succinct computational secret sharing schemes for graph access structures and adaptively-secure flexible broadcast encryption in the standard model, both with optimal parameters. The main driver for both our results is a new construction of a compact programmable pseudorandom set sampler (PPS), introduced by [Goyal and Yadugiri; CRYPTO'26], from standard Learning with Errors (LWE) assumption [Regev; STOC'05]. We show that PPS generically imply PPRGs with many useful properties and, moreover, by replacing PPRGs with PPS we can achieve full succinctness in the underlying applications to secret sharing and adaptive security compilers for broadcast encryption. This yields the $\textit{first}$ flexible broadcast encryption scheme in the standard model from $\textit{any}$ falsifiable assumption with fully compact ciphertext size, and a succinct computational secret sharing for evolving graph access structures with optimal share size from standard LWE.

item.title: Vector Commit-and-Reduce Schemes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2790
Authors: Anubhav Baweja, Pratyush Mishra, Tushar Mopuri, Bharath Namboothiry
Summary: Hash-based argument systems are seeing increasing adoption in practice, owing to their ease of deployment, fast provers, and plausible post-quantum security. However, they still lag behind elliptic-curve counterparts due to their large proof sizes and (comparatively more) expensive verifiers. Attempts to optimize these metrics have focused on one of the two ingredients underlying these arguments, namely Interactive Oracle Reductions, leaving the other ingredient, Vector Commitments (VC) schemes largely ignored. This is in part because Merkle trees are the best known hash-based VC scheme to date.
To make progress on this front, we introduce Vector Commit-and-Reduce (VCR) schemes. These generalize VC schemes by allowing both the commitment and opening algorithms to be interactive protocols, and moreover by allowing the opening algorithm to be a reduction instead of an argument. By requiring VCR schemes to satisfy strong round-by-round knowledge soundness notions, we show how they can be used to construct hash-based reductions from IORs. Our transformation extends prior work which used (non-interactive) VC schemes.
We also provide a construction of a VCR scheme, Canopy, that greatly reduces proof size and verifier time by reducing the vector opening claims to proximity claims about certain (committed) codewords. This latter feature enables us to use a wide variety of techniques for proving, batching, and accumulating these claims, and indeed we use these to obtain both concrete and asymptotic improvements for hash-based arguments and reductions.
For SNARKs based on the Bolt code [CRYPTO 2026], we reduce proof sizes by 50\% and verifier hashes by $3\times$ with only a 5-15$\%$ prover overhead. For SNARKs based on the Reed-Solomon code, we reduce proof sizes by 20$\%$, and verifier hashes by $1.5\times$ with only a 20$\%$ prover overhead. We also construct hash-based Proof-Carrying Data where the recursion overhead is $O(\lambda \sqrt{\log N})$ hashes; in comparison, the state-of-the-art requires $\Omega(\lambda {\log N})$ hashes.

item.title: SETH: Subcode Equivalence in the Head
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2789
Authors: Marco Baldi, Michele Battagliola, Rahmi El Mechri, Laura Mattiuz, Marco Rinaudo, Paolo Santini, Riccardo Schiavoni, Edoardo Signorini
Summary: The Multi-Party Computation in the Head (MPCitH) paradigm has proven to be a versatile tool to design post-quantum digital signature schemes. Recently, MPCitH was improved with Threshold Computation in the Head (TCitH) and Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation in the Head (VOLEitH). In this paper, we propose two polynomial models for the Subcode Equivalence Problem (SEP) and derive TCitH and VOLEitH signatures from them. The resulting scheme has better performance when compared to other SEP-based signature schemes and also features shorter signatures when compared to other schemes based on similar assumptions.

item.title: Differentially Private Distance-Sensitive Representations for General Metrics
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2788
Authors: Paul Cesaretti
Summary: A distance-sensitive set representation stores a set $S$ from a metric space $(U,d)$ and answers queries of the form "is some element of $S$ within distance $r$ of $q$?''. Existing differentially private constructions are confined to Hamming space, because they route the query through a signature map built for that metric. We give a framework that removes this restriction. The released object records only the occupancy of a fixed public partition of $U$, so privacy transfers unchanged from an off-the-shelf private membership structure, and the entire metric dependence collapses into one packing quantity, the straddle number $\kappa$: the largest number of cells a ball of radius $r$ can meet. Any metric admitting a partition of width at most $(c-1)r$ and straddlenumber $\kappa$ then has an $\varepsilon$-differentially private $(c,r)$-representation with $\varepsilon =\ln(2\kappa/\alpha)$ in $O(k\log(\kappa/\alpha))$ bits.
Instantiating $\kappa$ gives matching upper and lower bounds in $\ell_\infty$ for partition-based constructions ($\varepsilon=O(\log d)$ at $c=\Theta(d)$, against $\varepsilon=\Omega(d)$ at constant $c$), and a randomized, dimension-free construction for every $\ell_p$ (one probe and $\varepsilon=\ln(2/\alpha)$ regardless of $d$) at the cost of a weaker, non-oblivious guarantee whose price is exactly this $\log d$ gap. For metrics available only through a distance oracle, we build the partition from a public net and a public navigable graph, and show that greedy search on that graph both locates and enumerates the cells a query must probe; on a $\lambda$-doubling metric this gives $\varepsilon\le 5\ln\lambda+\ln(2/\alpha)$. We further show that the per-query form of the guarantee is forced rather than chosen: any representation correct on all queries simultaneously requires $\varepsilon\ge\ln M+\ln(1/\alpha)-O(1)$ for $M$ the packing number of the whole space, and on doubling metrics this is achievable up to an additive $O(dim_D\log\frac{c}{c-1})$. Finally, the space bound is optimal in $k$ and $\alpha$.

item.title: Symbolic forward secrecy analysis of ML-KEM
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2787
Authors: Varsha Jarali, Shashi Kant Pandey
Summary: Post-quantum Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (KEMs) rely on generic transformations to achieve active security. Specifically, ML-KEM (FIPS 203) applies the Fujisaki--Okamoto (FO) transform to a lattice-based public-key encryption scheme, Kyber.CPAPKE, to construct an IND-CCA2 secure key exchange protocol, ML-KEM. While NIST standards and associated special publications discuss guidelines for establishing larger shared keying material using ML-KEM, formal symbolic proofs to evaluate these operational setups remain sparse. This work addresses this gap by conducting a formal symbolic analysis of ML-KEM using \textsf{ProVerif}. First, we verify the core primitive, establishing symbolic proofs for session key confidentiality, key agreement soundness, and Fujisaki--Okamoto implicit rejection fallback secrecy. Second, we examine the temporal security guarantees of ML-KEM under long-term static key leakage. Using \textsf{ProVerif}'s global phase constructs, we demonstrate that standalone static ML-KEM does not preserve Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS), rendering repeated static encapsulation for additional key share establishment vulnerable to retroactive decapsulation. Lastly, we formally model and verify that deploying ML-KEM with ephemeral key rotation or ratcheting mechanisms mitigates this vulnerability, providing robust forward secrecy and complete session domain separation.

item.title: Quantum Key Exchange from Public Quantum Money
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2786
Authors: Eli Goldin, Tomoyuki Morimae
Summary: Two-message quantum key exchange (2QKE) cannot be realized in a statistically secure way, and therefore some computational assumptions are required [Malavolta and Walter 2024]. So far, the known weakest assumption for 2QKE is the existence of one-way functions (OWFs): Malavolta and Walter constructed (even everlasting-secure) 2QKE from OWFs [Malavolta and Walter 2024], and Kitagawa, Morimae, Nishimaki, and Yamakawa constructed quantum public-key encryption (QPKE) with quantum public keys, which implies 2QKE, from OWFs [Kitagawa, Morimae, Nishimaki and Yamakawa 2024]. Can we construct 2QKE from a weaker assumption than OWFs? In this paper, we give the first complete characterization of 2QKE. We show that the following four primitives are (existentially) equivalent: everlasting-secure 2QKE, standard 2QKE, efficiently-verifiable state puzzles (EV-StatePuzzs), and one-time secure digital signatures with quantum signatures and signing keys. Because EV-StatePuzzs are potentially weaker than OWFs [Kretschmer, Qian and Tal 2025], the equivalence implies that 2QKE are potentially weaker than OWFs. Moreover, our result shows the equivalence between standard 2QKE and everlasting-secure 2QKE, which means that everlasting security comes for free. Finally, one-shot signatures, quantum lightning, and public-key quantum money mini-schemes imply EV-StatePuzzs, and therefore, our result also gives a new lowerbound, namely everlasting-secure 2QKE, of these public-key unclonable primitives. We also show that one-shot signatures imply QPKE with quantum public keys [Kitagawa, Morimae, Nishimaki and Yamakawa, 2024] constructed QPKE with quantum public keys from OWFs, and it was open whether QPKE with quantum public keys can be constructed from an assumption weaker than or incomparable to OWFs. Our result gives a potential answer to this question since one-shot signatures seem to be incomparable with OWFs. Moreover, QPKE constructed from one-shot signatures has an additional functionality, which we call certified freeze, that allows the receiver to publish a publicly verifiable classical certificate that computationally binds the receiver to an upper bound on the total number of distinct valid ciphertexts under its verification key.

item.title: Optimal Early-Stopping Broadcast via Exponential Information Gathering
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2785
Authors: Giovanni Deligios, Fatima Elsheimy, Simon Holmgaard Kamp, Ivana Klasovita, Chen-Da Liu-Zhang, Julian Loss, Charalampos Papamanthou
Summary: Early-stopping broadcast protocols guarantee termination based on the actual number of malicious parties, $f \leq t$, encountered during execution, rather than the worst-case scenario of $t < n$ corruptions. The seminal work of Dolev, Reischuk, and Strong~[JACM'90] established that $\min\{f+2,\, t+1\}$ rounds are necessary. The influential works of Berman, Garay, and Perry~[WDAG'92] and Abraham and Dolev~[STOC'15] introduced the first protocols achieving this optimal bound in the $t < n/3$ (unconditional, no setup) regime, while Perry and Toueg~[Tech.\ Report'84] gave the first protocol for the $t < n/2$ setting (with plain PKI), achieving $2 \cdot \min\{f+2,\, t+1\}$ rounds. Despite this early progress, closing the gap to the optimal bound in the computational setting has remained a longstanding open problem, and only recently has progress been made. The best known result in the $t < n/2$ regime is due to Elsheimy, Loss, and Papamanthou~[Eprint'25], achieving $f + O(\sqrt{f})$ rounds. In the dishonest-majority regime, the best known result is due to Deligios, Klasovita, and Liu-Zhang~[Eurocrypt'25], who obtain the first asymptotically optimal protocol, with $O(f)$ round complexity, for $t = (1-\epsilon)n$, where $\epsilon > 0$ is a constant.
In this work, we advance the state of the art in two directions. First, in the $t < n/2$ setting with plain PKI, we present a broadcast protocol in which all parties output within optimal $\min\{f+2,\, t+1\}$ rounds. Second, we complete the picture by introducing the first protocol that is optimally resilient ($t < n$) and asymptotically matches the lower bound for any number of corruptions $t < n$. By leveraging exponential information gathering (EIG) graphs, our constructions establish that these round bounds are achievable, providing the first feasibility result for optimal-round protocols, albeit at the cost of exponential communication complexity.

item.title: Privacy-Preserving Multi-Institutional Clinical Prediction via Multiparty Encrypted Newton-CG Logistic Regression
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2784
Authors: Xiaokang Dai, Weijie Miao, Wenyuan Wu, Yong Feng
Summary: Multi-institutional clinical prediction can benefit from larger and more diverse patient populations, but privacy and data-governance constraints often prevent pooling patient-level records. This study aims to enable collaborative logistic-regression training while keeping such records local. We developed a framework combining multiparty Cheon–Kim–Kim–Song (CKKS) homomorphic encryption with Newton–conjugate gradient optimization. Each institution computes local gradient and damped Hessian contributions, while only encrypted fixed-dimensional statistics are aggregated. The global Newton system is solved by encrypted preconditioned conjugate gradient with diagonal preconditioning and delayed division, making the dominant homomorphic cost depend mainly on model dimension. We evaluated the framework on nine clinical-prediction tasks from NHANES 2017–2018 and on the PIMA Diabetes and Breast Cancer Wisconsin datasets. Across the nine NHANES tasks, mean absolute deviations from pooled-data plaintext Newton training were below 0.002 for area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, area under the precision–recall curve, and average precision. Five-fold cross-validation accuracy was (77.21 ± 1.28)% on PIMA Diabetes and (96.42 ± 1.44)% on Breast Cancer Wisconsin. Under a common 20-iteration budget, the proposed method achieved approximately 3.85× faster training and nearly 90% lower peak memory use than a reproduced multiparty encrypted first-order baseline, while attaining a lower final relative gradient and closer agreement with plaintext Newton. These results show that exploiting locally computed Newton statistics can preserve predictive utility while substantially reducing encrypted training cost, supporting privacy-preserving multi-institutional clinical prediction without pooling patient-level data.

item.title: Bridging Correlation Measures and Unpredictability: Sharp Bounds and Insights for TRNG Validation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2783
Authors: Maciej Skorski, Onur Günlü
Summary: Do small correlations certify high unpredictability? We answer this for the high-order correlation measures (Mauduit and Sárközy) and finite-memory sources.
We develop minimax sharp bounds on next-bit prediction from high-order correlations and show that the min-entropy-rate deficit is linear in the largest correlation, with optimal first-order constants. We also bridge population and sample correlations through ergodic limits and finite-sample guarantees.
As an application, we show that the validation method for true random number generators recently proposed at WAIFI 2026 over-rejects: shrinking (sub-constant) thresholds strongly reject sources of nearly full entropy.

item.title: Memory-Efficient HQC Implementations on Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M7
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2782
Authors: Minjoo Sim, Siwoo Eum, Minwoo Lee, Seungwon Lee, Gyeongju Song, Lee Wai Kong, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Hwajeong Seo
Summary: In the Hamming Quasi-Cyclic (HQC) key encapsulation mechanism (KEM), eliminating the polynomial product buffer still leaves serialized inputs, operands, and candidate ciphertexts that may coexist during decapsulation. We organize storage around the last use of each value. Comparing each candidate component before producing the next allows both to share one workspace, while deterministic regeneration shortens the lifetimes of ephemeral supports. Our lifetime analysis relates the measured footprint to the values that coexist during reencryption in our compact design. We read dense operands directly from serialized inputs and reuse output storage as workspace before final serialization during key generation and encapsulation. These choices reduce overlapping storage across the complete KEM and complement established support-form and Zero-Buffer multiplication. We evaluate this organization for all three HQC parameter sets on ARM Cortex-M3 and Cortex-M7 under the August 2025 specification. In a cumulative Cortex-M3 HQC-256 comparison, combined representation and lifetime changes reduced the stack by 38.9% relative to a Zero-Buffer configuration that already uses component-wise ciphertext comparison. Using a separate configuration, we measured decapsulation footprints of 36,858 bytes on Cortex-M3 and 36,850 bytes on Cortex-M7, including peak operation stack and serialized input/output storage. The common object layout accounts for most of these footprints. In the evaluated configurations, the relative increase in decapsulation cycles from the direct to the compact implementation is larger on Cortex-M7 than on Cortex-M3. Retaining supports reduces cycles when memory permits. The kernels retain support-dependent control flow and memory accesses; we did not establish complete-KEM constant-time execution or physical side-channel resistance.

item.title: Exact $\ell_p$-CVP via Euclidean SVP in Polynomial Space
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2781
Authors: Jiseung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Hyung Tae Lee
Summary: We give a randomized, rank-preserving reduction from exact $\ell_p$-CVP to exact Euclidean SVP for every integer $p\ge2$. For rational inputs of bit length $\ell$ on full-rank lattices $L\subset\mathbb R^N$, the reduction uses $(Cp)^N\poly(p,\ell)$ oracle calls and additional bit operations, where $C$ is an absolute constant. It uses $\poly(p,\ell)$ working space outside the oracle, and all oracle queries have rank $N$ and $\poly(p,\ell)$ bit complexity.
For $p=2$, the reduction transfers polynomial-space exact SVP algorithms to exact CVP with $2^{O(N)}\poly(\ell)$ time overhead. Instantiating it with the SVP algorithms of Kannan and of Feng, Gao and Liu yields randomized polynomial-space CVP algorithms running in time $N^{N/(2e)+o(N)}$ and $N^{N/(4e)+o(N)}$, respectively. For every fixed integer $p\ge3$, the same reduction yields exact $\ell_p$-CVP algorithms for arbitrary rational targets either in randomized time and space $2^{O(N)}$, or in randomized time $N^{N/(4e)+o(N)}$ and polynomial space. These algorithmic bounds are up to polynomial factors in $\ell$.
The reduction performs local search sequentially over the cosets of \(2L\), where \(L\) is the input lattice, while tracking the excess of the current objective value over the optimum. Within a coset containing a closest vector, midpoint inequalities bound the unknown correction in terms of this excess, which in turn allows us to construct many short corrections that reduce the excess bound by a factor of four. A counting argument shows that these improving corrections form a sufficiently large fraction of the lattice points in a known search region, and a sparsification-based sampler assigns sufficiently large probability to every nonzero vector in that region, using at most one SVP call per sample.
Repeating this improvement over polynomially many stages yields exact recovery. For \(p\ge3\), the same framework is extended using a diagonal weighted norm computed from the current point.

item.title: Structured Quantum Hardness from Unstructured Assumptions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2780
Authors: Xiao Liang, Takashi Yamakawa, Chak Fai Yung
Summary: Whether useful structured hardness can arise from unstructured assumptions is a fundamental question in complexity and cryptography. The longstanding Bennett–Gill question asks whether $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ remains hard relative to a random oracle; [GIKKLS, STOC 2023] recently gave a conditional affirmative answer in the classical setting. We establish the quantum analogue: if $\mathsf{UP}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}$, then $\mathsf{NP}^{O}\cap\mathsf{coNP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}^{O}$ with probability $1$ over a random oracle $O$.
Beyond extending the classical result, this separation has a distinctly quantum significance: Shor’s algorithms defeat canonical number-theoretic hardness candidates, while lattice assumptions and other leading post-quantum cryptographic assumptions do not directly supply hard languages with two-sided classical certification on every input. Our conditional oracle separation provides evidence that such structured quantum hardness can nevertheless arise from unstructured sources.
Complementing this result, we rule out fully black-box quantum reductions of worst-case quantum hardness in $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ to post-quantum injective one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation. This barrier excludes a broad class of black-box approaches to deriving structured quantum hardness from generic cryptographic primitives, providing partial evidence that the non-black-box techniques in our first result are essential.

item.title: Optimizations and First-Order Masking of AIMer on Cortex-M4
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2779
Authors: DongCheon Kim, Jaeseung Han, Dong-Guk Han, Seog Chung Seo
Summary: We optimize AIMer-128f on Cortex-M4 and propose first-order masking of its signing. Since squaring is a Frobenius map about $\times 16$ cheaper than multiplication, we restructure AIM2's inverse-Mersenne S-box into a Frobenius-shifted addition chain, cutting multiplications per S-box from 24/23 to 9/10. Since one multiplication-check operand is constant across $N = 16$ parties, we build the partial-product table once and reuse it. Both are orthogonal to single-multiplication acceleration, and with a Radix-16 multiplier on NUCLEO-L4R5ZI, keygen/sign/verify drop 18.55%/3.94%/7.30%. 1-PINI gadgets on every sensitive operation give first-order probing security. TVLA finds no first-order leakage in 100,000 traces. Masking costs $\times 10.5$, itself improved 5.20%.

item.title: Breaking $\mathsf{TraintoDefend}$ via Adaptive Neuron Clustering in Cryptanalytic Model Extraction
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2778
Authors: Haojie Wu, Haolin Liu, Tianshuo Cong, Guoyan Zhang
Summary: Cryptanalytic model extraction poses a fundamental threat to deep learning model confidentiality by enabling precise parameter recovery with theoretical guarantees of functional equivalence. To counter this growing threat, $\mathsf{Train to Defend}$ (NeurIPS 2025) was proposed as the first dedicated defense against cryptanalytic extraction and remains the only defense believed to be effective to date. It encourages neurons to learn similar weights so that they switch activation states together, making their individual contributions harder to distinguish. However, we notice that neurons with similar weights need not switch activation states together under small perturbations. Instead, weight similarity can cause the original clustering rule to merge signatures from distinct neurons when only a subset of their normalized weight coordinates agree. Motivated by this observation, we introduce $\mathsf{SimBreak}$, an adaptive clustering rule that breaks the weight-similarity defense of $\mathsf{Train to Defend}$. $\mathsf{SimBreak}$ estimates a relative scale from all jointly observed weight coordinates and uses the same scale to test both weight direction and bias consistency. Across six protected fully connected networks trained on MNIST, $\mathsf{SimBreak}$ raises target layer signature recovery from $0\%$ to $100\%$, with a maximum relative recovery error of $2^{-22.27}$. Our work challenges the use of neuron weight similarity as a sufficient basis for protection and establishes adaptive evaluation as essential to assessing cryptanalytic extraction defenses.

item.title: Tamper-Resilient Quantum Key Encapsulation with Coherent Ciphertexts from qOWFs in the QROM
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2777
Authors: Shiyu He
Summary: Kitagawa et al. (CRYPTO 2024) constructed the first tamper-resilient, chosen-ciphertext-secure public-key encryption from quantum-secure one-way functions (qOWFs). However, their construction assumes authenticated classical channels and measures intermediate signed-phase states to produce classical ciphertexts. Therefore we ask whether coherent quantum ciphertexts can support active security and certified deletion over unauthenticated classical and quantum channels.
We construct the first tamper-resilient quantum key-encapsulation mechanism (QKEM) from qOWFs with coherent quantum ciphertexts and genuine validity-feedback confidentiality in the quantum random-oracle model. Our scheme, designated Signed-Fourier QKEM, retains signed coherence through honest encapsulation to form a state-consuming quantum ciphertext. Aside from an authentic root verification key, all transmitted classical metadata and quantum registers are subject to arbitrary adversarial tampering and entanglement. With one quantum public key per independent signing domain and a challenge serial unused in pre-challenge decapsulation queries, we prove session-key confidentiality under genuine different-header decapsulation, including queries sharing the challenge serial, and genuine same-header validity feedback. We also establish fixed-header key robustness against adaptive decapsulation attacks, bounding wrong-key acceptance by a negligible probability.
Furthermore, our scheme provides publicly verifiable computational certified deletion, protecting session-key privacy against subsequent, complete exposure of the receiver's secret state. Finally, composing our QKEM with a classical one-time private data encapsulation mechanism yields header-restricted chosen-ciphertext confidentiality for arbitrary polynomial-length messages.

item.title: One-Way Functions and Local Descriptions of Random Data
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2776
Authors: Dimitrios Myrisiotis
Summary: Sample compression describes a labeled sample by retained examples and extra information from which a decoder recovers the labels. We show that estimating the length of the shortest such description of random data is hard on average if and only if one-way functions exist. As in Hirahara and Nanashima's (FOCS 2023) consistent pointwise programs, the decoder labels each sample point separately, as a hypothesis does, but in our main result the labels are random rather than given by a concept. To label a point, it sees only that point, the retained examples with one extra bit each, a program, and a public random string revealed before the description is chosen. The length counts the choice of retained examples, their extra bits and the program, not the examples themselves. The task is to output a number between the $1/2$ and $3/4$ quantiles of the shortest length over the public string, up to an additive $a\lceil\log_2m\rceil$ for $m$ points and a fixed integer $a\ge0$. The main result takes polynomially many, at least $8n$, uniform $n$-bit points with independent uniform labels and any large enough polynomial time bound per query. If one-way functions exist, every efficient randomized algorithm fails to output such a number for all large $n$ with probability above an inverse polynomial that is the same for all algorithms and time bounds. Otherwise, for every inverse polynomial, some such algorithm fails with at most that probability for infinitely many $n$. For hardness, labels derived from one-way functions look random yet have short local descriptions, which random labels rarely have. The converse inverts a function that generates descriptions. One-way functions also exist if and only if estimating between the quantiles is hard, at some suitable time bound, for some PAC-style samplable data of the same sizes, labeled by a concept independent of the points.

item.title: Quadratic Extractors
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2775
Authors: Gautam Chandrasekaran, Jesse Goodman, David Zuckerman
Summary: A quadratic source is a random variable $X\sim\mathbb{F}_2^n$ generated by applying $n$ quadratics to a hidden uniform string. Previously, the best-known explicit extractor for this model required min-entropy roughly $k=n-\sqrt{\log n}$. In this paper, we give an explicit construction for min-entropy $k=\mathrm{polylog}(n)$. Even for the special case of $2$-local sources, where each bit of $X$ depends on two hidden uniform bits, achieving an entropy requirement below $k=\sqrt{n}$ was an important open problem. This is because such sources provably cannot be reduced (in a black-box manner) to our most powerful general-purpose seedless extractor, known as a sumset extractor. Our new extractor bypasses this barrier, providing the first explicit construction to go beyond sumset extraction.

item.title: Separating Pseudorandom Codes from Quantum Random Oracles
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2774
Authors: Nico Döttling, Anne Müller, Mahesh Sreekumar Rajasree
Summary: Pseudorandom codes (PRCs) combine two seemingly conflicting goals: robustness to noise and computational indistinguishability from random strings. Recent work has shown that classical symmetric-key PRCs over binary alphabets cannot be constructed from minimal cryptographic assumptions, such as one-way functions, via black-box reductions. In this work, we revisit this question in the presence of quantum computation and quantum information. We first consider pseudorandom codes with classical codewords but quantum algorithms. We prove that symmetric-key pseudorandom codes robust to Bernoulli noise admit no black-box construction from quantum random oracles, and hence from quantum-secure one-way functions. This establishes that the classical black-box barrier for PRCs persists even in the quantum computational setting. Motivated by this separation, we investigate the notion of quantum pseudorandom codes (QPRCs), in which codewords are quantum states and security is defined via computational indistinguishability from Haar-random states. We then present several positive results. Assuming quantum-secure one-way functions, we construct QPRCs that are secure against a single encoding query, allow multiple copies of the challenge state, and tolerate an error rate matching that of any classical uniquely decodable binary error-correcting code against a dephasing or bit-flip channel. We also show that the PRFS with proof of destruction due to Behera et al. (TCC 2023) can be extended to a 0-bit QPRC that is secure against multiple encoding queries and tolerates unbounded phase errors but only a constant number of bit-flip errors. Finally, assuming the existence of quantum-secure single-query pseudorandom states (1PRS), we construct single-query single-copy QPRC that tolerate arbitrary Pauli noise up to the decoding radius of a quantum error-correcting code with unique decoding.

item.title: Vectorized (2, 2)-Isogenies in the Theta Model Using AVX-512 and Applications to SQIsign
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2773
Authors: Marius A. Aardal, Diego F. Aranha, Patrick Longa, Giacomo Pope
Summary: Higher-dimensional isogenies have emerged as a powerful building block for isogeny-based cryptography, with recent protocols such as SQIsign relying on the efficient evaluation of $(2^n, 2^n)$-isogenies. Despite their attractive security and compactness properties, these schemes remain computationally expensive and improving their performance is an important step for their real-world use. In this work, we present a high-performance AVX-512 implementation of two-dimensional isogenies that effectively exploits their data-level parallelism. We develop a code generator that produces efficient AVX-512 implementations of arithmetic over $\mathbb{F}_p$ and $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$ for Montgomery-friendly primes of the form $p=c\cdot 2^e-1$ with $e\approx \log_2(p)$, covering the family of primes used by several protocols based on two-dimensional isogenies, including SQIsign. Building on this arithmetic, we vectorize the $(2^n, 2^n)$-isogeny formulas by Dartois et al. (ASIACRYPT 2024), achieving significant speedups over the corresponding, highly-optimized scalar implementation that uses x86-64 assembly. As an application, we accelerate the Round 2 version of SQIsign verification and obtain speedups of $2.5\times$ at NIST security level I and $3.2\times$ and $3.3\times$ at levels III and V, respectively. Our code generator also readily supports the larger primes of Round 3 SQIsign, for which we obtain verification speedups between $3.1\times$ and $3.4\times$.

item.title: STIR/SHAKEN: A Cocktail of Cryptographic Clumsiness
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2772
Authors: Josh Brown, Matthew Hardeman, Paul Grubbs
Summary: Scams and fraudulent robocalls are rampant in the telephone system. Fraudsters often employ call spoofing to impersonate a known caller to the victim, making it difficult to detect and block the fraudster’s calls. In an effort to combat call spoofing, the U.S. government in 2019 mandated the use of a new suite of protocols called STIR/SHAKEN. In STIR/SHAKEN, providers include a cryptographically-signed assertion about the caller’s identity and other metadata in call headers. This serves both to authentically convey this metadata between providers during call routing and to provide reportable, verifiable evidence of bad behavior by providers that originate fraudulent calls. This paper asks whether STIR/SHAKEN achieves its security goals, and at what cost to the telephone system. On security we find serious structural weaknesses: a year of STIR/SHAKEN certificates observed in production call traffic shows a PKI riddled with noncompliance—nearly half of valid certificates violate the specifications—a provider can prevent later verification of a STIR/SHAKEN assertion by taking its certificate offline, and a header-malleability flaw, which we verified in test calls placed with the help of a real telephone provider, causes a spoofed caller ID to be displayed as verified on some phones. The cost, meanwhile, has been steep: STIR/SHAKEN deployment has created systemic new harms to the privacy of all phone users. These new privacy harms take two forms. First, signing call metadata renders it cryptographically non-repudiable: for the first time in the phone system’s 150-year history, there is publicly verifiable proof that a call took place. Second, STIR/SHAKEN’s complexity pushes providers to outsource signing and verification—roughly half of the 29 providers we surveyed do so, most to a handful of dominant vendors—causing widespread new leakage of sensitive call metadata to off-path third parties. (One such off-path third party, Neustar, was acquired in 2021 by TransUnion, one of the three nationwide U.S. credit bureaus. Neustar authenticates over 30 billion calls per month—and TransUnion sells a “Phone Behavior Intelligence” product advertising “insight into billions of call transactions” obtained through its “deep carrier relationships.”) These structural harms sit atop implementation failures: our tests also found implementations that completely break the federally-mandated *67 caller-privacy mechanism. Finally, we propose solutions to the problems we identify. To fix the PKI, STIR/SHAKEN should adopt certificate transparency; a public certificate log also stops providers from taking certificates offline to defeat later verification. Our remaining solutions are cryptographic, and share a prerequisite STIR/SHAKEN cannot currently meet: the origin provider must learn the destination provider’s public key. We thus design a backwards-compatible key discovery mechanism that uses SIP error messages. We then attack the privacy harms directly: replacing STIR/SHAKEN’s signatures with asymmetric message franking (AMF) makes call metadata deniable again, and issuing AMFs blindly keeps it hidden from outsourced signers. We design the first blind signing protocol for the AMF construction of Tyagi et al., along with new security definitions capturing requirements novel to the setting, such as verifier-hiding blindness. To our knowledge, we thereby initiate the formal study of blind signing for designated-verifier signatures; we believe this is of independent interest.

item.title: Can Fully Homomorphic Encryption on Public Blockchains Protect Sensitive Medical Consultations? A Security and Privacy Assessment
Sumcheck bit packing
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2770
Authors: Matteo Frigo, abhi shelat
Summary: Circuit-based zero-knowledge proofs over large fields waste most of a field element when they commit to a single bit. We study the problem of committing to packed witnesses, in which $m$ bits are stored in one element of $GF(2^m)$, while still allowing the proof system to verify linear claims about the individual bits.
Prior approaches to this problem either (a) scale to packing only 4 bits[Fs24], (b) require tensor-structured claims and additional sumcheck rounds that incur larger soundness error [DP23,DP25], or (c) rely on Frobenius automorphisms [Koc26]. In contrast, we present a simpler reduction that exploits only the $GF(2)$-linearity of the field trace and achieves soundness error $2^{-m}$ for arbitrary bit-linear claims. We then use a characterization of trace-zero field elements to make the reduction zero-knowledge over any hiding linear commitment scheme: whereas previous constructions verify $O(m^2)$ or $O(m)$quadratic constraints in the commitment scheme, our protocol requires only linear constraints.

item.title: Projective Jet Geometry and Hold-Out Rank of Binary Goppa Codes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2769
Authors: Yongge Wang
Summary: We develop a projective-geometric and algebraic framework for the higher-order polynomial relations among the public generator-matrix columns of a binary Goppa code, the relations exploited by the recent structural distinguishers and key-recovery methods for Classic McEliece. The alternant representation realizes the public columns as rational points on a hidden curve parametrized over $\F_{2^m}$; higher-order vanishing conditions become fat-point conditions, pulled back along the hidden parametrization.
Our first contribution is an exact characterization of a codimension-$t$ ambient space containing all products of $d$ code polynomials: the products satisfy $(\pi^dh)'\equiv0\pmod{g^2}$ for the support polynomial $\pi$ and the Goppa polynomial $g$, and the space of degree-$\le dD$ polynomials with this property has dimension $dD+1-t$ once $dD\ge2t-1$. Equality with the actual product space is proved in a local regime, verified computationally on every instance tested, and stated as a conjecture. Our second contribution is a Frobenius-descent theorem: a binary form vanishes on the hidden curve if and only if it vanishes on the union of its $m$ Frobenius conjugates, with the $\F_2$-dimension of such forms equal to the $K$-dimension of the ideal of the union; from it we derive Hilbert-function bounds, including a multilinear version attained on all but one of the twenty-seven keys with $t\ge5$ tested (and missed by one on that key), and the local structure of the pulled-back forms at the roots of $g$.
We then analyze the universal dependencies among Hasse-jet conditions in the multilinear setting of the attacks: a closed formula for the rank at a single column, and an explicit family of $\binom{k}{2s-d-2}$ relations between the conditions at any two columns. At a held-out column we prove an exact codimension formula for the Goppa subcode generated by the gradients of the vanishing forms. Finally, running our experimental pipeline (the jet system of the attacks, without the key-recovery steps) on six independently generated keys of a Classic-McEliece-shaped code shows that the kernel dimension is comparable to that of a random control, while every kernel form exhibits the predicted hidden-curve vanishing, the gradients span the predicted subcode, and the first-order normal data of the kernel is nearly independent of the key. Together these results explain the main components of the nuisance space of the recent attacks and isolate the conjectures that remain for an exact description of the kernel.

item.title: HqcLethe: Streaming HQC Encapsulation for Tiny Stateless Servers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2767
Authors: Wind Wong, Klaus v. Gleissenthall
Summary: Stateless post-quantum authenticated key exchanges such as post-quantum WireGuard hedge against unexpected cryptanalytic advances by combining a lattice KEM with code-based Classic McEliece. However, recent attacks have led Germany's BSI to advise against McEliece, which leaves these protocols with lattices alone. HQC, the code-based KEM that NIST selected, could restore diversity, but its keys do not fit in a single packet, so a server would have to buffer multi-packet handshakes. This would leave an attack surface for memory exhaustion, which is what WireGuard's stateless handshake was designed to avoid in the first place. McTiny demonstrated that stateless key encapsulation for Classic McEliece is possible by streaming key blocks one-at-a-time. However, HQC's encapsulation does not split as easily into individual packets, as cyclic polynomial multiplication, unlike matrix-vector multiplication, is inherently non-local.
We present HqcLethe, a stateless key exchange that streams an HQC encapsulation in packet-sized pieces. It uses the Chinese remainder theorem to split the polynomial multiplication into independent remainders, one per packet, and masks them so that they reveal no more than an ordinary HQC ciphertext, which we prove in Rocq with SSProve; we also verify session secrecy, server authentication and forward secrecy in ProVerif. Client puzzles bound CPU exhaustion, and HqcLethe removes memory exhaustion: on a Raspberry Pi 3B+, each worker runs in a fixed 1.2-1.6 MiB. At category 5 it sends 27x fewer bytes and uses 9.0x less server CPU than McTiny, the earlier stateless code-based design.

item.title: Keyber: Recovering the Signal by Amplifying the Noise in ML-KEM
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2766
Authors: Vipin Kumar, Prathamesh Ram, Suparna Kundu, Dhiman Saha
Summary: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is now being deployed in real-world applications to provide security against adversaries with quantum computers. Therefore, the resistance of ML-KEM’s implementations to physical attacks requires thorough evaluation. So far, fault attacks on ML-KEM have targeted the decapsulation operation. The key generation operation has received little attention from a fault-attack perspective.
In this work, we present Keyber, the first statistical ineffective fault attack (SIFA) on the key generation of ML-KEM. Keyber is a key-recovery attack that needs only a single fault in key generation. The fault adds a known value to the error vector. Thus, the public key becomes faulty, while the seed of the public matrix remains intact. Every subsequent decapsulation, therefore, carries a known induced error. The adversary encapsulates locally and keeps only ciphertexts whose induced error peaks at exactly one coefficient. A decapsulation failure can then be attributed to that coefficient. Each query yields one linear inequality on the secret key, with no further faults.
We observe that approximately 0.2-27% of encapsulations are usable for different parameter sets of ML-KEM. The full secret key is recovered using up to 30,000 inequalities across all security levels. We also realise the attack for ML-KEM-512 on an ARM Cortex-M4 device using a single over-clock fault. We then recover the entire secret key end-to-end. A single fault in this one-time operation thus compromises the key for its entire lifetime. Protecting ML-KEM, therefore, demands hardening not only decapsulation, but also key generation.

item.title: Cryptanalysis of Pairing-Based Additive Masking with Prime-Field Secrets
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2768
Authors: Harliv Singh
Summary: We analyze the public values generated by a pairing-based multi-secret sharing construction in which each secret is added to a power of a common pairing value. The secrets lie in the prime subfield of the extension field containing the public values. We show that the first two public values determine the common mask whenever an explicit nonzero condition holds. We also show that the exceptional case is resolved for the parameter set considered in the numerical example. Consequently, the complete public transcript determines every secret, without requiring a participant share or an initially compromised secret. We further describe two related forms of leakage: recovery of all secrets after disclosure of one suitable secret, and a reduction in the possible values of a secret from a single public value. Our conclusions concern the field-valued, common-base masking construction analyzed here; they do not imply that pairing-based secret sharing in general is insecure.

item.title: BASTION: Lock-Step, Staggered and Sequential Share Schedules for a First-Order Masked ML-KEM NTT on FPGA
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2765
Authors: Marcos Lázaro Díaz
Summary: The Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) is the arithmetic core of ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and a prominent side-channel target in hardware. Because the transform is linear, first-order arithmetic masking applies share-wise without fresh randomness, which leaves one design decision open: when each share is processed. Published designs process the shares in sequence on one datapath, or on one datapath per share started a configurable delay apart and in random order; running both datapaths in lock-step is the third option. We implement the three schedules on one first-order masked NTT core for ML-KEM on Artix-7 and measure their cost and pre-silicon leakage under one synthesis flow. An iso-architectural unmasked control separates the cost of masking from that of parallelisation: the delivered lock-step core costs 1.56x the LUTs, 2.33x the slices and twice the DSPs of the control at an unchanged cycle count and 196.1 instead of 227.3 MHz, while the sequential core needs 9 LUTs more than the control at twice the cycles. We state when a set of samples combines both shares of a secret, measure the criterion on the RTL and use it as a cycle-accurate oracle. On a whole-design toggle model that sums both share domains, calibrated with injected flaws detected within 750 traces, no schedule leaks at first order in five pairs of runs of 10^5 traces. At second order the schedules form a scale: the lock-step core leaks in single samples, the sequential core only at the pair of samples that its public offset relates, and the staggered core in both ways at every delay we tested short of one transform. Every detected sample lies in the support view of the oracle, which flags up to 80% of the samples of a window for the univariate test, and some lie outside its form view, so lazy reduction matters. A check on the routed netlist finds no cell shared by the domains of the lock-step and staggered cores, and finds the cells that synthesis shares once the preservation attributes are removed. Silicon validation is left to future work.

item.title: Trapdoors Beyond Inversion: Recoverable Information in Public-Key Cryptography
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2764
Authors: Kanad Chakravarti, Shreyas Gupta, Bhavana Kanukurthi, Girisha Shankar
Summary: Classical trapdoor functions recover complete preimages, whereas public-key decryption needs only designated information about an encryption input. We study this distinction through trapdoor hardcore functions (TDHFs), whose trapdoor recovers a prescribed value $h(x)$ from a public evaluation $f (x)$, while $h(x)$ remains pseudorandom given the public key and evaluation. For perfectly correct primitives, we show that adaptive TDHFs characterize IND-CCA2-secure public-key encryption. The constructive direction requires only a single recoverable bit and allows noninjective public evaluations. Extending the rejection-sampling approach, we show that adaptive pseudorandomness itself controls queries to unselected candidate evaluations, without requiring full inversion. We also prove that lossy TDHFs characterize lossy public-key encryption, identifying statistical hiding of the designated recovered value as the relevant lossiness requirement. Fiber samplability together with fiber hiding yields a parameter-preserving correspondence with lossy encryption and, through the known long-message transformation, almost-always lossy trapdoor functions when the recovered-value length exceeds the fiber-sampling randomness length. Ordinary TDHFs provide the corresponding characterization of IND-CPA encryption. Together, these results make explicit the roles of adaptive recovery, conditional sampling, and randomness costs in transformations between public-key encryption and full-inversion primitives.

item.title: On Key Recovery from Exposed Neural XOR Activations in DES and TDES
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2763
Authors: Kwangjo Kim
Summary: We study the security of natural ReLU realizations of the Data Encryption Standard (DES) and two-key Triple DES (TDES) when an adversary can submit non-binary inputs and observe selected intermediate neural values. The attack exploits the piecewise-linear extension of XOR: paired inputs that differ in one expanded right-half bit reveal the corresponding round-key bit from the change in a natural XOR node. For DES, the resulting 48-bit first-round subkey leaves only the eight key-schedule bits omitted by PC-2; enumerating these bits and checking an intermediate value recovers the 56-bit effective master key. For two-key EDE TDES, the same technique recovers the first encryption subkey of K_1 and the last DES subkey used by the middle decryption under K_2; two independent 2^8 completions then recover the full 112-bit key pair. The exposed round subkey is recovered with a constant number of leakage observations per bit, giving query complexity linear in the targeted subkey length; the remaining searches are fixed-size for DES. Python experiments report exact recovery for 1,000 random DES keys and 1,000 random two-key TDES key pairs. These results concern a synthetic intermediate-oracle model for natural neural implementations and do not claim a physical attack on conventional DES/TDES hardware or software.

item.title: AirBB: Lightweight Threshold Anonymous Credentials without Random Oracles from BB Signatures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2762
Authors: Sebastian Faust, Jonas Hofmann, Philipp-Florens Lehwalder, Hussien Othman
Summary: Anonymous credentials are a well-studied cryptographic primitive enabling users to prove statements about their identity and selectively present personal information in an unlinkable manner. The issuer, however, is often a single point of failure. Threshold issuance addresses this by distributing the issuer across several parties such that a quorum of them must cooperate to issue credentials. Numerous constructions of single-issuer and threshold issuance anonymous credentials have been proposed. However, existing schemes each have at least one of the following weaknesses: (1) their presentations depend on the number of attributes, (2) they are not concretely efficient, or (3) they rely on the random oracle model (ROM) for non-interactive presentations.
In this work, we present a new construction of threshold anonymous credentials that has a constant presentation size of 240 bytes, rivals the efficiency of BBS, and does not rely on the random oracle model. We achieve this by combining techniques from set commitments with Boneh-Boyen (BB) signatures (Eurocrypt'04) and prove our scheme's security in the algebraic group model. This is on par with the tight security proofs of existing schemes, which typically rely on the AGM or GGM, or on assumptions justified in those models. Since signing uses linear operations, the scheme is easily thresholdizable, without requiring interaction between the issuers or preprocessing.

item.title: Superlattice methods for the shortest vector problem and discrete Gaussian sampling
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2761
Authors: Minki Hhan, Jiseung Kim, Sunyeop Kim, Thijs Laarhoven
Summary: We give worst-case algorithms for the shortest vector problem (SVP) and discrete Gaussian sampling (DGS) at arbitrary widths. Both algorithms generate lists on a dense superlattice and combine vectors along a chain down to the input lattice. Random shifts let us control the expected number of representations of a vector regardless of the lattice. For SVP we balance these counts with a novel midpoint-shell test to ensure output distributions are sufficiently uniform. For DGS we use Gaussian weights and correct the probabilities of selecting entries from the final list.
For SVP, our optimized algorithm runs in time $2^{0.409 n+o(n)}$ and space $2^{0.259 n+o(n)}$, improving the best $2^{n/2 + o(n)}$ worst-case SVP complexities of Hhan [ePrint, 2026]. For Haar-random lattices, or assuming a natural upper bound on the kissing constant, the costs of the algorithm match the $2^{0.292 n+o(n)}$ time and $2^{0.208 n+o(n)}$ space of Becker-Ducas-Gama-Laarhoven [SODA 2016].
For quantum SVP, through a series of refinements and generalizations we obtain worst-case time and space $2^{0.247n+o(n)}$. This improves the best known heuristic quantum SVP time complexity of $2^{0.256n+o(n)}$ due to Bonnetain-Chailloux-Schrottenloher-Shen [Eurocrypt 2023], without requiring any heuristic assumptions.
For discrete Gaussian sampling, we provide a sampling algorithm at any width with distribution error $2^{-\kappa}$, running in worst-case time $2^{0.292 n+o(n)} \operatorname{poly}(\kappa)$ and space $2^{0.208 n+o(n)} \operatorname{poly}(\kappa)$, improving upon the previous best $2^{n + o(n)}$ cost for sampling at arbitrary widths of Aggarwal-Dadush-Regev-Stephens-Davidowitz [STOC 2015].
As further applications, we obtain fast algorithms for approximate-SVP/CVP, bounded distance decoding, and estimating the Gaussian mass and smoothing parameter of any lattice.

item.title: Syndrome Decoding out of the Head: Structure-Aided Side-Channel Witness Recovery on SDitH
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2760
Authors: Jaeyeon Lee, Jaeho Jeon, Young-Sik Kim
Summary: Regular syndrome decoding (RSD) underlies several code-based signature schemes, including SD-in-the-Head (SDitH). Its secret witness has exactly one nonzero coordinate per block, and the selected positions must satisfy a public syndrome equation. In this work, we show how these structural constraints can be exploited to recover the complete witness from imperfect side-channel information.
We present a profiled power analysis of the witness-embedding operation in the SDitH Round-3 reference implementation. We train convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to classify the mux digits encoding each regular block and use their outputs to rank candidate positions. To correct errors in these predictions, we combine the resulting rankings with the public syndrome and the regularity constraints. We formulate this recovery problem as an affine correction system with block-validity constraints and analyze its rank, consistency, and uniqueness for the systematic parity-check matrix used in SDitH. Based on this analysis, we develop a quotient-syndrome decoder that identifies blocks whose true positions fall outside the initial candidate lists, avoiding exhaustive enumeration of block subsets.
We evaluate our attack on an ARM Cortex-M4 using measured power traces. With a single target trace per key, our approach recovers all 100 test witnesses under -Os using 4,000 profiling traces, and 91 out of 100 under -O3 using 16,000 profiling traces. Each successful recovery matches all 616 serialized witness bits. These results demonstrate how the regular structure of RSD and the public syndrome can compensate for imperfect side-channel predictions, thereby enabling full-witness recovery.

item.title: Differentially Oblivious Graph Ball Queries
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2759
Authors: Zimai Guo, Cheng Hong, Zhechen Li
Summary: A graph ball query returns all vertices within distance $r$ of a source vertex. On $N$-vertex graphs with maximum degree at most $\Delta$, ordinary breadth-first search answers such queries with $O_{\Delta,r}(1)$ record accesses. These accesses depend on private edges and can reveal graph structure. Full obliviousness hides this dependence, but incurs substantial overhead. Differential obliviousness (DO) [Chan et al., SODA'2019] trades off between privacy and efficiency by relaxing full obliviousness to $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy on the access traces of neighboring graphs.
We study DO graph ball queries under three widely-adopted edge-level neighboring relations: add/delete, replacement, and $2$-switch. Starting from padded adjacency records, we charge all observable accesses, including preprocessing. For fixed $\Delta,r\ge2$, error probability $0<\beta<1/2$, and $0\le\delta\le(1-2\beta)/2$, we prove an $\Omega_{\Delta,r,\beta}(1+Ne^{-\varepsilon})$ expected lower bound at every sufficiently large connected graph and every public source. For every fixed $r\ge2$, we give $(\varepsilon,0)$-DO sampling algorithms with expected cost $O_{\Delta,r,\beta}(1+Ne^{-\varepsilon/C})$ using constant size of hidden workspace, where $C$ depends only on $\Delta,r$ and the neighboring relation. Especially, for $r=2$, we have $C=1$, which indicates that the algorithm achieves the tight bound under all three relations. Finally, we consider repeated queries on the same graph, where the cost of protected preprocessing can be amortized across queries. For fixed $\Delta,r,\beta$, we construct a linear-size reusable index with $(\varepsilon,0)$-DO preprocessing and constant query cost. The expected preprocessing cost is linear in $N$ when $\varepsilon$ exceeds a sufficiently large constant multiple of $\log N$.

item.title: Fine-Grained Proof Complexity for Elementary Arithmetic in Extended Frege
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2758
Authors: Andrew Krapivin, Jiatu Li, Elaine Shi
Summary: Proof complexity has historically focused on qualitative results, such as whether natural mathematical statements (e.g. the Pigeonhole Principle) admit polynomial-size proofs in certain proof systems (e.g. Resolution or Frege). In contrast to the rich theory of algorithm design, there is little understanding of how to design quantitatively efficient proofs. We initiate the study of fine-grained propositional proof complexity. Our motivation comes from an emerging line of cryptographic constructions such as the elegant work of Jain and Jin (2022), in which the efficiency of the resulting scheme is governed by the size of the underlying Extended Frege proofs.
Our main result is that the basic laws of integer arithmetic —commutativity and associativity of addition and of multiplication, together with distributivity — admit Extended Frege proofs of quasi-linear size, when addition is implemented by the schoolbook algorithm and multiplication by an FFT-based algorithm. This seemingly elementary result turns out to be surprisingly non-trivial: the natural paper-and- pencil arguments for distributivity and for associativity of multiplication translate into Extended Frege proofs of quadratic size. To reach quasi-linear size, we develop a technique we call index generalization, which we believe will find wide application in the design of efficient propositional proofs.

item.title: Affine Advantage in Guess-type Attacks on Goldreich’s PRGs: Generalization, Characterization and Countermeasures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2757
Authors: Ximing Fu, Mo LI, Shihan Lyu
Summary: The recent guess-type attack (Eurocrypt'26) on Goldreich's pseudorandom generators exploits the strong bias toward constants that can arise when some inputs of majority-based predicates are fixed. This attack has demonstrated substantial effectiveness against several concrete parameter instances (Eurocrypt'24\&'25, Asiacrypt'24). In this paper, we generalize this attack paradigm to arbitrary affine approximations, characterize its capabilities, and develop a new predicate as a countermeasure.
We introduce a guess-and-affine-approximation (GAA) attack framework that generalizes existing guess-type attacks from constant approximations to arbitrary affine approximations of residual nonlinear predicates. To characterize the capacity of GAA attack, we introduce the bit-fixing affine advantage $\operatorname{adv}_{b'}(M_b)$, defined as the maximum affine advantage of a $b$-ary nonlinear predicate $M_b$ over all residuals with $b'$ unfixed inputs. For polynomial stretch $m=n^s$ and logarithmic nonlinear arity $b=\gamma\log_2 n$, we obtain the optimal attack complexities $C^\star$ linking bit-fixing affine advantages: (1) $C^\star>2^{cn}$ for every $c<2^{-(s-1)/\gamma}$ iff $\operatorname{adv}_{\theta b}(M_b)\to 0$ for every constant $\theta\in(0,1]$; (2) $C^\star=2^{o(n)}$ iff fixing only $o(b)$ predicate inputs can yield a residual with affine advantage $\frac{1}{2}-o(1)$, and the sufficient direction also holds for $b=\Omega(\log n)$. In particular, if $\operatorname{adv}_{b-r}(M_b) =\frac12- O\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)$ for $r\le s-1$, then $C^\star$ can further decrease to $n^{O(1)}$. These results complement prior analyses for arities $O(1)$, $\omega(1)\cap O(\log n)$, and $\Omega(n^{1/s})$.
Guided by the results above, we introduce the $\XOR_a$--$\MODtwelve_b$ family as a predicate candidate.
